## Overview

Andalusians are the people of Andalusia, an autonomous community in southern Spain. They live mainly in the eight southernmost provinces: Almería, Cádiz, Córdoba, Granada, Huelva, Jaén, Málaga, and Seville. The region includes the valley of the Guadalquivir, the Baetic System, the Sierra Morena, the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, and cities including Córdoba, Granada, Málaga, and Seville. In January 2006, the region’s population stood at 7,849,799. Andalusian Spanish is recognized as a set of diverse Spanish dialects. Andalusian culture has been shaped by Tartessians, Iberians, Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Greeks, Romans, Vandals, Visigoths, Byzantines, Berbers, Arabs, Jews, Romanis, Castilians, and Gitanos. Flamenco, Holy Week, cuisine, and Hispano-Moorish architectural styles are among its best-known cultural expressions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

### Architecture

Hispano-Moorish architectural styles are described as largely Andalusian in origin. Córdoba was the capital of Al-Andalus during the Islamic Golden Age and became a prominent center of education and learning. The sources also describe Atlantic-facing harbors as important through trade with the New World.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Andalusian music history does, however, name instruments associated with historical transmission through Andalusia, including the rebec, guitar, naker, adufe, alboka, anafil, exabeba, atabal, atambal, balaban, sonajas de azófar, xelami, shawm, dulzaina, gaita, rackett, geige, and theorbo.

## Music & performance

Andalusian music includes traditional and modern genres originating in Andalusia. The most famous are *copla* and flamenco. Flamenco is a form of music and dance mostly performed by artists and ordinary people from Andalusia, and the term is sometimes used for several regional musical traditions.

Improvised flamenco songs of ancient Andalusian origin are called *cante jondo*. They are characterized by reduced tonal ambiance, strict rhythm, baroque ornamentation, and repetition of notes, and are sung by a single singer, the *cantaor*. Flamenco songs are divided into *cante jondo* and *cante chico*: the former is slower and commonly concerns disappointed love or death, while the latter is quicker, more popular, and dance-oriented. The concept of *duende* describes a spiritual or emotional bond between performer and audience created through intense concentration and passion.

Named flamenco styles include *fandango*, *fandangos de Huelva*, *granadínos*, *malagueñas*, *saeta*, *sevillana*, *siguiriyas*, *soleares*, and *Tangos*. The guitar is a vital instrument, marking the measure and accompanying expressive solos called *falsetas*. Ramón Montoya was an influential early guitarist; his successors included Manolo Sanlúcar and Paco de Lucía.

The golden age of flamenco is given as 1869 to 1910. Musicians performed at bars called *café cantantes*, including Café de Chinitas in Málaga. In 1956, Hispavox released *Antología del Cante Flamenco*, and the first national *cante jondo* competition was held in Cordoba. Nuevo Flamenco later emerged from developments associated with Camarón de la Isla and Paco de Lucía.

Historical accounts also connect Andalusia with the transmission of Near-Eastern musical instruments. The rebec is associated with the Maghreb *rebab*, the guitar with *qitara*, and the naker with *naqareh*. Other named instruments include the *al-duff*, *al-buq*, *al-nafir*, *al-shabbaba*, *al-tabl*, *al-tinbal*, *sunuj al-sufr*, *sulami*, *zamr*, *al-zurna*, and *tarab*.

## Dance & theatre

Flamenco is the principal named Andalusian dance tradition in the sources. It developed in Andalusia and the Americas during the 19th and 20th centuries and is performed with several song forms, including *cante jondo* and *cante chico*. The *cante chico* styles are described as particularly dance-oriented. *Sevillana* is listed among the flamenco styles. They also do not distinguish a separate ceremonial dance repertoire from entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

Holy Week, or *Semana Santa*, is identified as an important element of Andalusian traditional culture and is shared with other Hispanic countries in America and the Philippines. Spanish Catholic religion is described as a traditional vehicle of Andalusian cultural cohesion. The different regions of Andalusia have developed distinctive customs, while sharing a connection to Catholicism as it developed during Baroque Spanish society.

Andalusia Day is celebrated on 28 February and commemorates the 1980 autonomy referendum. The sources also mention the popular religious song *Santo Dios*, sung at harvest time by peasants and day labourers in the provinces of Málaga, Seville, and Huelva. Its melody inspired the anthem of Andalusia.

## Foodways

Andalusian cuisine is the regional cuisine of Andalusia, Spain. Its influences include Christian, Muslim, and Jewish traditions. The oldest known cookbook associated with it, *Kitab al tabij fi-l-Maghrib wa-l-Andalus fi `asr al-Muwahhidin, li-mu'allif mayhul*, dates from the 13th century.

Olive oil is central to frying and is produced mainly in Jaén, Córdoba, Seville, and Granada, with smaller production in Málaga, Almería, Cádiz, and Huelva. Foods prepared *a la Andaluza* are dredged in flour, sometimes chickpea flour, and fried in a large quantity of hot olive oil. Fish and shellfish are important because Andalusia has access to both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. Named seafood includes white shrimp from the Bay of Cádiz, prawns, murex, anchovies, baby squid, cuttlefish, flounder, and *bocas de la Isla*, a dish from San Fernando using a local crab. Tuna is used in *atún encebollado*, while *ortiguillas* are sea anemones in batter.

Named dishes include *pescaíto frito*, *gazpacho*, Cordoban *salmorejo*, *pringá*, oxtail, *jamón ibérico*, prepared olives, *alboronía*, *poleá*, anise, *pestiños*, *amarguillo*, *polvorones*, lard bread, wine doughnuts, *torrija*, and *calentitos*. The *jamones* of Jabugo, Valle de los Pedroches, and Trevélez are specifically noted.

Wines include sherry and the wines of Jerez, *manzanilla* of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, white wines of Cádiz, *paxarete*, wines of Condado in Huelva, Montilla-Moriles wines, Málaga wine, and *la tintilla* of Rota. Named liquors include *anís* made in Rute and Cazalla de la Sierra, and rums from the Tropical Coast of Granada.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources connect Andalusia with poetry and song. One historical account states that troubadours derived their sense of form and the subject matter of their poetry from Andalusia, while also describing a hypothesis that the troubador tradition developed through contact with Moorish arts during the Reconquista. Arabic song from the second half of the 9th century is mentioned in connection with this discussion.

The sources name the female troubadours, Ramón Menéndez Pidal, Meg Bogin, William VIII, Giammaria Barbieri, and Juan Andrés. Flamenco preservation and transformation are described as continuing in the modern era, including efforts to preserve traditional melodies, rhythms, and instruments and to pass this cultural heritage to future generations.

## Language & religion

Andalusian Spanish is described as a set of diverse Spanish dialects spoken in Andalusia. The sources also distinguish the Andalusian language movement, which seeks recognition of Andalusian as a language different from Spanish; Andalusi Arabic, formerly spoken in Iberia; and Andalusi Romance, also called Mozarabic, a Romance language spoken in Al-Andalus.

Catholicism is described as a major element of Andalusian cultural cohesion. The region’s history and culture have also been influenced by Muslim and Jewish traditions, and Andalusian cuisine reflects Christian, Muslim, and Jewish historical influences.
